title: How do you trace a request across multiple microservices (distributed tracing, correlation IDs, centralized logging)?
shortTitle: How do you trace a request across multiple microservices

s1_definition.profdef: Tracing a request across microservices means following a single logical operation as it flows through many services so you can see the full path, timing, and outcome end to end. The three pillars are a correlation ID (a unique identifier generated at the edge and propagated through every service and log line for that request), distributed tracing (a trace composed of spans, one per operation, linked by trace and span IDs and propagated over headers, visualized in a tool like Jaeger or Zipkin), and centralized logging (shipping all services' logs to one searchable store like the ELK stack so you can query by correlation ID). Together they let you reconstruct exactly what happened to one request across the whole system.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a customer's loan application at the National Bank of India passes through many departments: reception, verification, credit check, approval, and disbursement. If something goes wrong, you cannot figure out where unless every department stamps the same case number on the file and logs what they did with it. The correlation ID is that single case number written on the folder the moment it enters the building, carried by hand to every department. Distributed tracing is the detailed timeline showing exactly how long the file spent in each department and in what order, like a stopwatch log per desk. Centralized logging is the central records room where every department files a copy of its notes, all searchable by that one case number, so an auditor can pull the complete story of that one application from a single place instead of walking to five departments.
s1_definition.oneliner: Stamp every request with a correlation ID at the edge, propagate trace and span IDs across services so a tracing tool can show the end-to-end timeline, and ship all logs to one place searchable by that ID.

The three pillars are a correlation ID (a unique identifier generated at the edge and propagated through every service and log line for that request), distributed tracing (a trace composed of spans, one per operation, linked by trace and span IDs and propagated over headers, visualized in a tool like Jaeger or Zipkin), and centralized logging (shipping all services' logs to one searchable store like the ELK stack so you can query by correlation ID). Together they let you reconstruct exactly what happened to one request across the whole system.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine a customer's loan application at the National Bank of India passes through many departments: reception, verification, credit check, approval, and disbursement. If something goes wrong, you cannot figure out where unless every department stamps the same case number on the file and logs what they did with it. The correlation ID is that single case number written on the folder the moment it enters the building, carried by hand to every department. Distributed tracing is the detailed timeline showing exactly how long the file spent in each department and in what order, like a stopwatch log per desk. **One line to remember:** Stamp every request with a correlation ID at the edge, propagate trace and span IDs across services so a tracing tool can show the end-to-end timeline, and ship all logs to one place searchable by that ID.

sections.s2_technical:
The fundamental problem is that in a monolith a single stack trace tells the whole story, but in microservices one user action fans out into calls across many independently running services, each with its own logs, so no single log file contains the full picture. To reconstruct what happened you must tie all the pieces together, and that tying is done with identifiers that travel with the request.

A correlation ID, sometimes called a request ID, is a unique value generated once, usually at the API gateway or the first service that receives the request. It is then attached to the request as it flows onward, typically in an HTTP header, and every service includes it in every log line it writes for that request. Because the same ID appears in every relevant log across every service, you can later search all logs for that one ID and see the complete journey. The essential rule is generate once at the edge and propagate everywhere, never regenerate it downstream.

Distributed tracing is the richer, structured form of this. A trace represents the whole end-to-end request and is identified by a trace ID. Within a trace, each unit of work, such as a single service handling the request or a single database call, is a span, identified by a span ID, and each span records a parent span ID so the spans form a tree showing causality and nesting. Spans carry start and end timestamps, so the trace reveals not just the path but the latency contribution of each hop, which is how you find the slow service. The context, meaning the trace ID, span ID, and sampling decision, is propagated between services over standard headers, today usually the W3C `traceparent` header. Tools like Jaeger and Zipkin collect these spans and render a waterfall diagram of the request. In the Java and Spring world, Micrometer Tracing, formerly Spring Cloud Sleuth, instruments this automatically: it creates spans, propagates context over headers, and even injects the trace and span IDs into the logging pattern so your logs and traces line up. OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard for generating and exporting this telemetry.

Centralized logging is the third pillar and the place you actually search. Each service writes structured logs, ideally JSON, including the correlation or trace ID, and a shipper forwards them to a central store such as Elasticsearch, queried through Kibana, which is the ELK or Elastic stack, or alternatives like Splunk, Loki, or a cloud logging service. Centralization matters because without it you would have to log into each service's host or container to read logs, which is impossible across dozens of ephemeral Pods. With it, you paste one correlation ID into the search box and instantly get every log line from every service for that request, in order.

The three pillars work together, and the senior-level framing is that they map to the broader idea of observability through its signals: traces show the path and timing, logs show the detailed events, and metrics show aggregate health, all correlated by the same IDs. Practical nuances I always mention are that context propagation must cross asynchronous boundaries too, so when a service publishes to Kafka it should put the trace context in the message headers and the consumer should continue the same trace, otherwise the trace breaks at the queue; that sampling is used in high-volume systems to trace only a fraction of requests to control cost while still capturing enough to diagnose issues, often with tail-based sampling to keep the traces that errored or were slow; that logs should be structured and include the trace ID so they can be pivoted directly from a trace in tools that integrate the two; and that you must standardize on one propagation format, ideally W3C Trace Context and OpenTelemetry, so every service and third-party library speaks the same language and the trace is never lost at a boundary.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India, a single transfer request flows through the gateway to the transfer service, which calls the account service and the fraud service, and then publishes a notification event. One day transfers were intermittently slow, and the on-call engineer could not tell which service was responsible.

Problem 1 — each service logged to its own file with no shared identifier, so correlating a single slow transfer across four services meant manually eyeballing timestamps across four log streams, which was hopeless. This is exactly why a correlation ID is needed: one ID stamped at the gateway and written in every log line lets you pull the whole story with a single search.

Problem 2 — even with a correlation ID, the engineer could see the request touched all four services but not which hop was slow. This is exactly what distributed tracing adds: spans with start and end times show the latency of each hop, so the slow service stands out immediately in the waterfall.

Problem 3 — the slowness sometimes happened after the transfer committed, during the asynchronous notification, and the trace stopped at the Kafka boundary. This is exactly why trace context must be propagated through message headers so the consumer continues the same trace.

The mini-project builds a `TraceContext` carrying trace and span IDs, a `Tracer` that starts child spans and records timing, a `CorrelatedLogger` that stamps every log line with the trace and span IDs, and simulated `GatewayService`, `TransferService`, `AccountService`, and `FraudService` plus a Kafka-style async step that propagates context. The demo processes one transfer, shows the correlation ID flowing through every service and log line, shows spans timing each hop so the slow one is visible, and shows the trace continuing across the async notification.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the tracing demo
java -cp target/classes com.bank.tracing.TracingDemo

# In a real Spring Boot service, add Micrometer Tracing + an exporter:
#   implementation 'org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-actuator'
#   implementation 'io.micrometer:micrometer-tracing-bridge-otel'
#   implementation 'io.opentelemetry:opentelemetry-exporter-otlp'
# Then view traces in Jaeger and search logs in Kibana by traceId.
docker run -d -p 16686:16686 jaegertracing/all-in-one   # Jaeger UI at :16686
curl -H "traceparent: 00-<traceId>-<spanId>-01" http://localhost:8080/api/v1/transfers
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: one transfer request for fifty thousand from Rajesh (SAV2001) to Priya (CUR3001), flowing through the gateway, transfer, fraud, and account services and then an asynchronous notification.

Step 1: The request hits the gateway, which generates a correlation ID once at the edge, equal to the trace ID, and logs its first line stamped with that trace and span ID. This single ID is now the case number for the whole journey.

Step 2: The gateway calls the transfer service, passing the context. The transfer service starts a child span under the gateway's span, continuing the same trace, and logs that it received the transfer, again stamped with the same trace ID but a new span ID, so the logs for this hop are tied to the request yet distinguishable as a separate step.

Step 3: The transfer service calls the fraud service, which starts another child span and logs its scoring line with the same trace ID. This hop deliberately takes about a hundred twenty milliseconds, and when its span ends it records that duration.

Step 4: The transfer service then calls the account service, which starts its own child span, logs the debit and credit, and ends quickly at about fifteen milliseconds. Now the trace has two sibling child spans under the transfer span, one slow and one fast, with their durations recorded.

Step 5: The transfer service publishes a notification event, and critically it puts the trace context into the message header as a traceparent value, so the asynchronous consumer can continue the same trace rather than starting a new one. The trace does not break at the Kafka boundary.

Step 6: Back at the gateway the response is returned, still logging the same correlation ID. To debug the earlier slowness, the engineer searches the centralized logs for that one correlation ID and sees every line from every service in order, and the trace waterfall in Jaeger shows the fraud scoring span as the clear latency culprit at a hundred twenty milliseconds, which pinpoints exactly where to optimize.

```
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    [trace=a1b2c3d4 span=11111111] GATEWAY received transfer; correlationId=a1b2c3d4
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    [trace=a1b2c3d4 span=22222222] received transfer SAV2001 -> CUR3001 amount 50000
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    [trace=a1b2c3d4 span=33333333] scoring SAV2001 amount 50000
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    SPAN end op=fraud.score trace=a1b2c3d4 span=33333333 parent=22222222 durationMs=120
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    [trace=a1b2c3d4 span=44444444] debit SAV2001 credit CUR3001 amount 50000
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    SPAN end op=account.debitAndCredit trace=a1b2c3d4 span=44444444 parent=22222222 durationMs=15
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    [trace=a1b2c3d4 span=22222222] published notification event with traceparent=00-a1b2c3d4-55555555-01
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    [trace=a1b2c3d4 span=11111111] GATEWAY returning response for correlationId=a1b2c3d4
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    To debug, search centralized logs (Kibana) for correlationId=a1b2c3d4
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    The trace waterfall (Jaeger) shows fraud.score was the slow hop (~120ms).
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Tracing a request across microservices is about following one logical operation end to end, and I build it on three pillars: correlation IDs, distributed tracing, and centralized logging. The problem they solve is that in a monolith a single stack trace tells the whole story, but in microservices one user action fans out across many independently running services, each with its own logs, so no single log file has the full picture. You have to tie the pieces together with identifiers that travel with the request.

The correlation ID is the simplest and most important starting point. It is a unique value generated once, usually at the API gateway, then attached to the request as it flows onward, normally in an HTTP header, and every service writes it into every log line for that request. The rule I always stress is generate once at the edge and propagate everywhere, never regenerate it downstream, because the whole value comes from the same ID appearing in every relevant log. With that, you search all logs for one ID and see the complete journey.

Distributed tracing is the richer, structured form. A trace represents the whole request and has a trace ID, and within it each unit of work is a span with its own span ID and a parent span ID, so the spans form a tree that shows causality and nesting. Because spans carry start and end timestamps, the trace reveals not just the path but the latency of each hop, which is how you find the slow service. The context is propagated between services over standard headers, today the W3C traceparent header, and tools like Jaeger or Zipkin render it as a waterfall. In the Spring world Micrometer Tracing, which used to be Sleuth, does this automatically, creating spans, propagating context, and injecting the trace and span IDs into the log pattern so logs and traces line up, with OpenTelemetry as the vendor-neutral standard underneath. Centralized logging is the third pillar and the place you actually search: every service writes structured JSON logs including the trace ID, a shipper forwards them to a central store like Elasticsearch, and you query by correlation ID in Kibana, because logging into dozens of ephemeral Pods individually is impossible.

This came up directly on our transfer platform when transfers were intermittently slow. At first each service logged separately with no shared ID, so correlating one slow transfer across four services was hopeless. Once we added a correlation ID at the gateway and distributed tracing, we searched the centralized logs for the one ID, saw every line from every service in order, and the Jaeger waterfall showed the fraud-scoring span as the clear culprit at around a hundred twenty milliseconds, which told us exactly where to optimize. We also found the trace was breaking at the Kafka boundary for the async notification until we propagated the trace context in the message headers so the consumer continued the same trace.

The nuances I mention to show depth are that context propagation must cross asynchronous boundaries by putting the trace context in message headers, that high-volume systems use sampling, often tail-based so you keep the traces that errored or were slow, to control cost, that logs should be structured and include the trace ID so you can pivot straight from a trace to its logs, and that you must standardize on one format, ideally W3C Trace Context with OpenTelemetry, so every service and library speaks the same language and the trace is never lost at a boundary. The one-line summary I give is: stamp every request with a correlation ID at the edge, propagate trace and span IDs across every service including async hops so a tool like Jaeger shows the end-to-end timeline, and ship all logs to one place searchable by that ID, and then any request becomes fully reconstructable.

---

keyPoints: Distributed tracing: Zipkin/Jaeger — follow request across services
Centralized logging: ELK/Loki — aggregate logs from all services
Metrics: Prometheus + Grafana — latency, error rate, throughput
Health checks and alerting: detect issues before users do
